content.thinking:
I'm putting the postmortem together now. The timeline shows the legacy-checkout-fallback flag was switched off at 04:29:13, the same moment the monthly-spend feature was switched on. Reverting monthly-spend is already ruled out, since the incident persisted, while reverting legacy-checkout-fallback back on is confirmed, which makes it the cause. The logs also show account pages moving from the legacy renderer to the new one.

I'm checking the mechanism now: the ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47 starting at 04:29 points to a divisor that is zero, and that explanation rests on the monthly-summary reading rather than on a direct check. The monthly-spend flag being off without relief makes me wonder whether the new renderer, not that flag, is what drives the monthly path. Account pages failed for a large share of shoppers.

I'm building the causal chain now, starting with shoppers' account page requests failing and tracing back through the ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47 to the switch-off of legacy-checkout-fallback. Monthly-spend-feature is already ruled out as the trigger, and no deploy shows up in the readback.

I'm checking whether any deploy lines up with the onset, and the change events for the day before show no deploy, only the two flag changes. The timing ties the cause to the flag switch-off at 04:29:13, so I'm building the step that dates that change to its row.

I'm checking the monthly-spend flag against the timeline: turning it off earlier didn't help, and I'm confirming the reversion of the legacy-checkout-fallback change still holds with monthly-spend left on. The step for that change dates it to 04:29:13. Then I'm pinning down the mechanism in the code path, where the monthly average divides by a count that is zero for shoppers who bought before but not this month.

I'm working out the causal chain for the postmortem, starting from the failing account page requests and tracing each cause back toward the flag switch-off at 04:29:13.

I'm laying out the causal chain step by step, from the failing account page requests down to the flag switch-off. The step that explains why the line raised ties it to the monthly path the new renderer takes, and the step after that says the account pages had moved onto that renderer at the onset.

I'm weighing how to structure the causal chain: the symptom first, then the ZeroDivisionError, then the move to the new renderer, the flag switch-off that caused it, and finally the zero-divisor mechanism in one sentence.

I'm laying out the last step of the chain: the new renderer's monthly spend summary divides by this month's purchase count with no zero guard, which is the bug that fails for shoppers who bought before but not this month.

I'm settling the wording of the root-cause explanation now: the new renderer's monthly spend summary divides by purchases this month without a zero guard, so shoppers who bought before but not this month hit the error and get a failed page.

I'm working out the contributing factors now. The first is that nothing before the change tested the new renderer's spend summary for a shopper with no purchases this month, so the fault could reach shoppers before anyone saw it.

I'm working through the contributing factors now. The first is that nothing tested the new renderer's spend summary with a shopper who has no purchases this month before the flag sent traffic there, so the fault reached shoppers unseen. The second is that the flag change applied to all traffic within the same minute, with no staged rollout that could have caught a small share of failures early. The third is that two flags were switched at the same moment by the same actor, which blurs which change caused the failure.

I'm weighing whether the nobody-paged point belongs among the contributing factors, since it's really about how the alert was routed, and I'm leaning toward treating it as its own detection gap rather than something that would have shortened the outage on its own.

I'm deciding where the alerting gap belongs: the alert paged nobody, but it's unclear that a page would have shortened the outage, so I'm keeping it under what went wrong rather than among the contributing factors. I'll also note the Mitigation Agent's first revert was quick, and when it was refuted it restored monthly-spend, leaving things as they were before moving on.

I'm checking the remaining items in the postmortem now: the investigation ranked the right flag second, so the first revert hit the wrong one and cost the wait. The Investigator's claim that monthly-spend enabled the spend summary path was refuted, and nobody was paged, which I'm keeping as its own detection gap.

I'm weighing what the lead effects section should say: the lead named the right flag, but the investigation ranked it second, so Argus reverted monthly-spend first. I'll also note that the assumptions depend on Code-Fix's reading of the source matching the revision that actually ran, and that monthly-spend's role in the failing path is inferred from the refuted mitigation rather than from the code.

I'm turning to the action items: the first is a requirement that switching on a flag which routes production traffic onto a new code path depends on that path's tests passing against ordinary account data, including accounts with past purchases but none this month. The second is to roll flag changes on io-shop out to a small share of traffic first.

I'm settling the action items now: a detection item to page on-call on the io-shop error-rate alert, and a guard to keep legacy-checkout-fallback on until the fix is merged, with neither tied to a specific contributing factor.

Now I'm writing up the went-well items, starting with the Mitigation Agent's quick first revert and its restoration of monthly-spend once that candidate was refuted, then checking the timing references against the onset window.

action_items.item: Before a feature flag on io-shop can send production traffic onto a new code path, require that path's tests to pass against ordinary account data, including an account with past purchases but none this month.
Roll out io-shop feature flag changes to a small share of traffic first, and widen them only after the error rate holds.
Stop a staged flag rollout on io-shop automatically and revert it when the service's error rate rises during the rollout.
Change feature flags on io-shop one at a time, with an observation window between changes.
Route the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop so that it pages the on-call engineer.
Keep legacy-checkout-fallback on until the fix under review in AI-2 is merged and deployed, and record that hold where flag owners will see it.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account page requests failed: the service's own account-page error-rate warning rose from its usual level, and the error-rate alert fired.
Account page requests were raising ZeroDivisionError in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py from the onset minute ({G5309.3}), and the account page handler turned each one into a failed page.

Account pages had moved from the legacy renderer to the new renderer, whose spend summary runs the line that raised. The legacy renderer's count was highest at {Gc27d.7} and the new renderer's at {Gc27d.11}.

ruled_out.what: The monthly-spend-feature flag, switched on at the same instant ({P2.1}): turning it off left the service at the incident's level, and the service came back with it still on once legacy-checkout-fallback was turned back on.
A deployment: the change events read for the day before the onset held only the two flag changes, and no deploy.

causal_chain.step: The legacy-checkout-fallback flag was switched off at {P1.1}. Flag evaluations went from all on before the onset to mostly off in the onset minute, and then to all off.

The new renderer's spend summary divides by the number of purchases the shopper made this month, and Code-Fix's reading of the source says that number is zero for an ordinary shopper who has not bought this month.

input.cause_in_plain_words: Switching off a setting moved the shop's account pages onto newer code that likely breaks for any shopper who has bought before but not this month, because it tries to work out an average over zero purchases.

contributing_factors.factor: No check was seen that tested the new renderer's spend summary with an account that has past purchases but none this month before a flag could send production account pages to it. Code-Fix's reading says the test file's own fixture calls such a shopper the ordinary case.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The divide-by-zero would have been found before the flag was switched off, and account pages would not have been sent to a path that fails for ordinary shoppers.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: Switching off legacy-checkout-fallback moved all account page traffic to the new renderer within the onset minute. No staged rollout of the flag change to a small share of traffic was seen.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Only a small share of account pages would have failed while the change was judged, and the rollout could have been stopped before it reached everyone.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: Two flags on the same service were changed by the same actor at the same instant, so the investigation could not tell from the record which one caused the errors.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The flag that set it off would have been the only change in the window, so the first revert would have targeted it and the incident would have ended sooner.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

lead_effects.effect: It did not change what was done: the investigation weighed it as unverified and ranked legacy-checkout-fallback second, so that flag was reverted only after the revert of monthly-spend-feature was refuted.

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent placed the onset in the minute both flag changes came, and the flag history it read surfaced both changes.
The Mitigation Agent reverted the top-ranked candidate's flag, monthly-spend-feature, which could be put back.
The Mitigation Agent put monthly-spend-feature back on when reverting it did not help, so the service was not left carrying a change that did nothing.
The Mitigation Agent turned legacy-checkout-fallback back on for the second candidate, and the service came back to normal.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as a draft pull request for a person to review.

went_wrong: The person's lead in the thread named the right flag before the investigation began, but the investigation ranked that flag second. The first revert went to the wrong flag, and the right one waited until that revert was judged.
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to the alert.

input.root_cause: In the files Code-Fix read, the new renderer's monthly spend summary (`average_spend_per_item_this_month` in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py, line {F1.1}) divides the account's spend this month by the number of purchases it made this month, and nothing guards against that count being zero. So for any shopper who has bought before but not this month it raises ZeroDivisionError, and `serve_account_page` catches the error and returns a failed page.
input.still_at_risk: If legacy-checkout-fallback is turned off again, account pages could go back onto the new renderer and fail again for shoppers with no purchases this month.
input.symptom: Shoppers' account pages failed to load
